exercises.prompt: OPTIONAL How the Rugby Game Works Rugby union is usually played on a grass-covered pitch 100 metres long and 70 metres wide (see diagram below). Each team has 15 players and a game lasts for 80 minutes. The game is played with an oval-shaped ball that players can kick, run with, or pass to teammates in order to score tries or kick goals.To score a try, worth five points, a player must carry the ball across the opposition's try line and ground it. His team's best kicker can then earn two more points for the conversion if he kicks the ball between the goalposts and over the crossbar. But scoring a try is not so easy. When an attacking team's players are running with the ball towards the try line, they are faced with a line of big, strong defenders who are experts at tackling. To get past these defenders, attacking players can pass the ball to each other until one of them finds a gap in the defence through which they can run to score a try. The ball can only be passed backwards or sideways, however; a forward pass is a foul that the referee should penalize.

exercises.prompt: Reading Text: Football Without Borders Football is the world’s most popular sport, played and watched by millions of people in every country. In international football, teams and officials come from many different cultures. To play and work together well, they must show cultural sensitivity. This means respecting different customs, gestures, and ways of communicating. For example, in some countries, it is polite to bow, while in others, players shake hands. Some teams pray before a match, and others sing loudly. Coaches and referees must understand these differences to avoid misunderstandings. During the World Cup, the host country welcomes teams from all over the world. They follow strict protocol for starting matches, greeting officials, and playing the national anthems. Good etiquette is important in post-match press conferences and media interviews. Players must also follow a code of conduct, showing respect to referees and fans. Interpreters often help teams from different countries communicate during training and games. One example is the 2022 World Cup in Qatar. The organizers trained volunteers and referees on cultural differences and provided information in many languages. Another case is the UEFA Champions League, where multinational teams work together every day and learn how to respect each other’s traditions. Football is more than a game—it is a global language that connects people. But to play it well, we must learn how to communicate across cultures.

Verb
Meaning
Example Sentence
Cross
To kick the ball from the side
of the field to the center
near the goal.
The winger crossed the ball
to the striker in front of the
goal.
Dribble
To move the ball forward by
kicking it lightly and
repeatedly while running.
Messi can dribble past many
players with ease.
Head
To hit the ball using your head He headed the ball into the
net to score a goal.
Mark
To stay close to an opponent
to stop them from receiving
the ball.
The defender marked the
forward tightly.
Pass
To kick the ball to a teammate She passed the ball to her
friend during the match.
Punch
For a goalkeeper: to hit the
ball with a fist to clear it
away.
The goalkeeper punched the
ball away during the corner
kick.
Save
To stop the ball from going int
The goalkeeper made a
great save in the final
minutes.
Score
To get a goal by putting the
ball into the net.
He scored the winning goal
in the last minute!
Shoot
To try to score by kicking or
striking the ball toward the
goal.
She shot the ball from
outside the box.
Tackle
To take the ball away from
an opponent using your feet.
The defender tackled the
player and won the ball.

"The Big Match"
Adam loves sports, especially football. Every weekend,
he plays with his friends in the park. He brings his own
ball and wears his lucky shoes. Before the game, they
always warm up by stretching and jogging. It helps them
avoid injuries.
During the game, they listen to the coach. He says things
like “Great job!” or “Keep running!” to support them. The
referee watches closely. If someone breaks a rule, the
referee gives a yellow card.
Adam plays hard and always respects his team. He
drinks water, eats healthy food, and gets enough sleep.
He wants to stay fit and strong. After the match, they all
shake hands to show respect. Sometimes they play with
teams from other schools, so they learn to respect
different customs.
One Saturday, a team from another town visited. They
spoke a different language, so the players used hand
gestures and smiles to communicate. Adam gave a
thumbs-up when someone scored. Everyone had fun,
and they took a group photo at the end.
Moral:
 Playing sports is not just about winning. It’s about
teamwork, health, respect, and having fun together.

"One Team, One Goal" (Football)
Youssef was selected to join his city’s youth football team
for an international tournament in Spain. It was the
biggest event of his life, and he was both excited and
nervous. The coach gave them a clear plan: train hard, stay
focused, and support one another on and off the field.
The team trained six days a week. Each session started
with a warm-up and light stretching to prevent injuries.
Then they practiced passing, dribbling, and team
strategies. Youssef wore a smartwatch to monitor his
heart rate and used a fitness app to record his progress.
“Train smart, not just hard,” the coach always said.
Before matches, the coach gave motivational talks.
“Communicate clearly,” he reminded them. “Use short
calls like ‘Man on!’ or ‘Switch!’ and respect the referee, no
matter what.”
When they arrived in Spain, Youssef noticed that some
teams didn’t speak English or Arabic. On the field, players
used simple gestures — a nod, a raised hand, a smile.
Before one match, the opposing team stood still during
the Jordanian national anthem. That small act of respect
meant a lot to Youssef.
During the semi-final, a player from the other team fell
and Youssef helped him up. After the game, the referee
praised both teams for their sportsmanship. Even though
Youssef’s team didn’t win the final, he felt proud.
He had improved his fitness, learned to work as part of a
team, and discovered that respect and fair play are more
powerful than winning.
Moral:
 Football is more than a game — it teaches discipline, unity,
and how to connect with others across cultures.

"Training for the Big Tournament"
Lina is a young basketball player preparing for her first
international tournament. Her coach believes she has
great potential, but to succeed, she needs to follow a
strict training and fitness plan.
Every morning, Lina trains with her team. They practice
passing, shooting, and running drills. After training, they
cool down with stretching exercises to avoid muscle
injuries. She uses a smartwatch to track her heart rate
and an app that records her daily steps and calories.
Technology helps her see her progress and improve her
performance.
She also eats a balanced diet and drinks plenty of water.
Recovery is just as important as exercise, so she sleeps at
least eight hours each night and takes rest days when
needed.
When Lina arrives at the tournament, she is nervous.
Teams from other countries are there, and not everyone
speaks the same language. On the court, players use
body language like nodding, thumbs-up, or simple hand
signals to communicate. Before each match, they shake
hands or bow, depending on the team’s culture.
One moment stood out: after a tough game, a player from
another team gave Lina a friendly smile and tapped his
chest – a gesture of respect. She smiled back. That small
moment showed how sports can build connection
without words.
Moral:
 Lina learned that international sports are about more
than winning. They’re about dedication, communication,
and respecting every player—no matter where they come
from.
